source.title_on_document: The current state of artificial intelligence generative language models is more creative than humans on divergent thinking tasks

supplement.where: No supplementary material in the article record (PMC flags has-supplement = no). Data availability: https://osf.io/xv6kh/
supplement.holds: The OSF repository holds the data; the article gives all reported statistics in the text and Tables 2 to 4.

paper_design_summary: 151 US adults on Prolific completed the Alternative Uses Task (fork, rope), the Consequences Task (no sleep, walking on hands), and the Divergent Associations Task without AI. The authors then collected 151 GPT-4 sessions on the same tasks, each told to give as many responses as the matched human gave on the timed tasks. Originality (semantic distance from the Open Creativity Scoring tool and the DAT score), elaboration, and word occurrence were compared between the human and GPT-4 groups.

studies.label: Humans vs GPT-4 on three divergent thinking tasks

participants.exclusions: The paper reports N = 151 human participants (Abstract; Methods, Human participation; Table 1). It also says participants who failed two attention checks were removed from all analyses (N = 2) and that 2 participants with fewer than 7 DAT responses were excluded from the DAT analysis. It does not say whether 151 is the count before or after these removals. The GPT-4 group is 151 sessions ('instances'), not people.
participants.who: Human participants recruited on Prolific (approval rating above 97 percent, proficient English speakers, born or resident in the USA; mean age 41.21), compared with 151 GPT-4 sessions run by the first author.
participants.quote: Human participants (N = 151) were recruited via Prolific online data collection platform in exchange for monetary compensation of $8.00.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 accessed through ChatGPT, one separate session per creativity measure; 151 sessions in total
ai_tool.how_used: No participant used AI. The first author prompted GPT-4 with the task instructions (AUT, then CT, then DAT), asking each session for the same number of responses as the matched human on the AUT and CT; GPT-4 output was compared with human output.

task.description: Alternative Uses Task (fork, rope), Consequences Task ('Imagine humans no longer needed sleep', 'Imagine humans walked with their hands'), and Divergent Associations Task (10 nouns as different from each other as possible).
task.duration: Humans: 3 minutes per AUT and CT prompt; DAT untimed (mean 126.19 s); whole survey on average 34 min (SD = 13.64). GPT-4: no time limit, fixed number of responses.

outcomes.name: AUT originality (semantic distance)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Open Creativity Scoring semantic distance (GloVe 840B, cosine between prompt and response vectors); fluency matched 1:1 between each human and a GPT-4 session. Analyzed with a 2 (group) x 2 (prompt: fork, rope) ANOVA. The paper reports 151 humans and 151 GPT-4 instances, with two prompts per source, but does not state the analyzed observation count for this outcome. The ANOVA error df is printed as 600; n_units is left null rather than substituting the combined source count or inferring an observation count from degrees of freedom.

contrasts.reported: Fork: human 0.79 (0.04) vs GPT-4 0.84 (0.02); Rope: human 0.68 (0.06) vs GPT-4 0.79 (0.02). Main effect of group F(1, 600) = 622.10, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.51; group x prompt F(1, 600) = 113.80, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.16; Tukey HSD: all pairs differ (p < 0.001) except human 'fork' vs GPT-4 'rope' (p = 0.989).
contrasts.locator: Table 3; Results, Primary results, Alternative uses task; Fig. 1

outcomes.name: CT originality (semantic distance)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Open Creativity Scoring semantic distance (GloVe 840B); fluency matched 1:1. 2 (group) x 2 (prompt: no more sleep, walk on hands) ANOVA; error df printed as 619. The analyzed observation count is not separately reported; n_units is left null rather than substituting the combined human/GPT-4 source count or inferring a count from degrees of freedom.

contrasts.reported: No more sleep: human 0.67 (0.05) vs GPT-4 0.71 (0.02); Walk on hands: human 0.67 (0.06) vs GPT-4 0.73 (0.01). Main effect of group F(1, 619) = 622.10, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.51; group x prompt F(1, 619) = 113.80, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.16 (the F, p, and η2 values are printed identically to the AUT ANOVA; only the df differ). Tukey HSD: all pairs differ (p < 0.001) except the two human prompts (p = 0.607).
contrasts.locator: Table 3; Results, Primary results, Consequences task; Fig. 2

outcomes.name: DAT score (mean pairwise semantic distance among one respondent's 10 nouns, x 100)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Divergent Associations Task score: average cosine distance over all pairs of a respondent's nouns, multiplied by 100 (OSF scoring). Measures semantic spread within one respondent's list, not across respondents. Independent-samples t-test.

contrasts.locator: Table 3; Results, Primary results, Divergent associations task

outcomes.name: DAT word occurrence across respondents (share of single-occurrence words)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Counts of DAT words that occur only once within a group's pooled responses (single occurrence) and words that occur in only one group (unique occurrence). Table 4 lists the 20 most frequent words per group (e.g., 'Elephant' 98 times for GPT-4 vs 'Dog' 28 times for humans). The paper does not print the total word count per group.

contrasts.reported: Single-occurrence words: humans n = 523 (69.92% of group responses) vs GPT n = 152 (47.95%). Words unique to one group: human 87.03% (n = 651) vs GPT 69.40% (n = 220). Overlap between groups 9.11% (n = 97). Group x word type: χ2 (1, N = 302) = 1.56, p = 0.211.
contrasts.locator: Results, Primary results, Divergent associations task; Table 4

diversity_detail.metric: Share and count of words occurring once within each group's pooled DAT responses; share of words occurring in only one group
diversity_detail.computed_over: All DAT words pooled within each group (human respondents; GPT-4 sessions)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Chi-square test of independence of group (GPT vs human) and word type (single vs unique occurrence), χ2 (1, N = 302) = 1.56, p = 0.211; no test of the single-occurrence share itself
diversity_detail.notes: Lower share of single-occurrence words means GPT-4 sessions repeated the same words more often, i.e., less diverse across sessions; direction is coded on diversity.

outcomes.name: Elaboration (words per valid response), AUT and CT
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Open Creativity Scoring elaboration (stoplist method); independent-samples t-tests. The AUT result is the contrast below; the CT result is also printed: GPT-4 M = 38.69, SD = 15.60 vs human M = 5.45, SD = 4.04, t(621) = -36.04, 95% CI [-35.04, -31.45], p < 0.001. The analyzed observation counts for AUT and CT elaboration are not separately reported; n_units is left null rather than substituting the combined human/GPT-4 source count or inferring counts from degrees of freedom.

contrasts.locator: Results, Primary results, Alternative uses task (elaboration paragraph) and Consequences task (elaboration paragraph)

outcomes.name: Fluency (valid response count), AUT, CT, and DAT
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of valid responses. For AUT and CT, each GPT-4 instance was prompted to supply the matched human's number of valid responses, after invalid human responses were removed; invalid or incomplete GPT-4 responses were then removed, and only valid responses in both groups entered analyses. The reported independent-samples t-tests therefore compare fluency under an imposed matching constraint. DAT asked for 10 nouns; Table 2 gives descriptive fluency statistics after retaining valid, legible responses, with no DAT fluency test reported. Analyzed observation counts for these fluency results are not separately stated and are not inferred from degrees of freedom.

eligibility.reason: Human task responses were scored for originality and elaboration with computed measures, so criterion 3 is met (Methods, Creativity measures; Results, Creativity scoring). The human sample is reported as 151, with two attention-check exclusions and two DAT-specific exclusions; these reported removals do not put it below 50, although the final analyzed count is not reconciled (Methods, Human participation; Divergent associations task; Procedure). GPT-4 responses were generated separately by the first author, and no people were randomly assigned to AI assistance, so criterion 1 fails and the study remains non-core ai_vs_human context (Methods, AI participation; Procedure).

one_line_finding: With fluency matched 1:1, GPT-4 (151 sessions) scored higher than 151 Prolific participants on semantic-distance originality in the Alternative Uses Task (group F(1, 600) = 622.10, η2 = 0.51) and the Consequences Task and on the Divergent Associations Task (84.56 vs 76.95, t(300) = 13.65; Table 3 and Results), but its DAT words repeated more across sessions (47.95 vs 69.92 percent single-occurrence words; Results, Divergent associations task).
